title: SafeHandle and leaks
sub: Native handles and objects that won't die
cards/0/title: When the resource is fully native
cards/0/body:
Sometimes P/Invoke hands you a raw OS handle, just an IntPtr number. It must be closed even if someone forgot to call Dispose.

You don't need to write your own finalizer for that: .NET has a ready-made wrapper, SafeHandle.
cards/1/title: Why SafeHandle beats your own finalizer
cards/1/body:
Its finalizer is critical: the runtime runs it with stronger guarantees than a regular one.

While a P/Invoke call is in progress, SafeHandle counts references, so the handle can't be closed mid-call. Otherwise the OS could hand the same number to another resource, and data would go to the wrong place (handle recycling).

All you have to write is ReleaseHandle().
cards/2/q: Why is closing a handle in the middle of a P/Invoke call dangerous?
cards/2/options/0: The OS may give the same number to a new resource, and the code writes data to the wrong place
cards/2/explain: Handle numbers get reused. SafeHandle won't let a handle close while a call is using it.
cards/3/options/0: FileStream, sockets and other wrappers over OS resources
cards/3/explain: SafeFileHandle, SafeSocketHandle, SafeWaitHandle: all of them derive from SafeHandle.
cards/4/title: Leaks happen even with a GC
cards/4/body:
The GC only removes what's unreachable. If something alive references an object you no longer need, that object will never die.

The classic case is subscribing to an event on a long-lived object. The event keeps a reference to the subscriber.
cards/4/code:
AppEvents.Changed += window.OnChanged;
// the window was closed, but never unsubscribed
cards/5/task: The window was closed: form.window = null. Run a collection and see whether Window dies. Then fix the leak.
cards/6/q: The window was closed, but memory keeps growing. The profiler shows a static event holding the window. What do you do?
cards/6/options/0: Unsubscribe from the event when the window closes
cards/6/options/2: Add a finalizer to the window
cards/6/explain: As long as the event references the window, the window is reachable. Neither GC.Collect nor a finalizer will help.
cards/7/q: What can keep an unneeded object alive? Select all that apply.
cards/7/options/0: A subscription to an event on a long-lived object
cards/7/options/1: A static cache collection that is never cleared
cards/7/options/2: A timer that references the object
cards/7/options/3: A local variable of a method that already returned
cards/7/options/4: A reference cycle between two garbage objects
cards/7/explain: A leak in .NET is always a path from a root to an object you don't need. Finished methods and garbage cycles don't create such a path.
cards/8/q: Someone forgot Dispose on an object with a SafeHandle. What happens next?
cards/8/items/1: The GC finds it and puts it on the finalization queue
cards/8/items/3: The next collection frees the memory
cards/8/explain: The resource does get released, just late. Dispose is always better.
